title: Child Safeguarding: Suspected Non-Accidental Injury Assessment and Referral

evidenceAudit.scope: Children under 18 with an injury where physical abuse is possible, in the emergency department (ED), primary care and paediatrics: alerting features, 'suspect' versus 'consider', documentation, imaging, Saudi reporting duties and safe disposition. Uses NICE NG76, the Saudi Law of Protection from Abuse regulations, the Saudi Family Protection Department and European Society of Paediatric Radiology (ESPR) imaging recommendations.
findings: Rebuilt from the thin 21 Oct 2026 version: NICE alerting features by injury type, the definition of an unsuitable explanation, Saudi reporting obligations and channels (1919), age-based imaging and six management steps added.
Saudi law makes reporting mandatory for any employee and every entity; this replaces the generic 'local law and policy' wording.
All statements trace to sources opened on 22 Oct 2026.
unverifiedSections: Hospital-based child protection centre procedures (National Family Safety Program) were not opened; follow the hospital child protection policy for the internal referral route.
Laboratory tests to exclude bone or bleeding disorders are mentioned by ESPR without a defined panel; no specific blood panel is given.
The Child Protection Law (Royal Decree M/14) text itself was not opened; reporting duties are cited from the Law of Protection from Abuse executive regulations.
Normal values for examination items are descriptive.

pathophysiology.summary: Inflicted injury produces patterns that do not fit the account, the child's development or a medical cause (NICE NG76, Section Unsuitable explanation). Infants who are not independently mobile rarely bruise accidentally, so bruising in them is an alerting feature (NICE NG76, Section Suspect physical abuse). Abusive head trauma, rib fractures and visceral injury may show no external marks (NICE NG76, Section Suspect physical abuse). A cultural explanation never justifies harm (NICE NG76, Section Unsuitable explanation).
keyMechanisms: Injury pattern inconsistent with the history or development (NICE NG76, Section Unsuitable explanation).
Bruising in a child who is not independently mobile (NICE NG76, Section Suspect physical abuse).
Occult injuries: rib fractures in infants, intracranial and visceral injury without marks (NICE NG76, Section Suspect physical abuse).
Fractures of different ages without a bone-fragility condition (NICE NG76, Section Suspect physical abuse).

symptoms: Delayed presentation after injury (NICE NG76, Section Suspect physical abuse — visceral injury).
Account that changes over time or differs between carers (NICE NG76, Section Unsuitable explanation).
Disclosure by the child — record exactly what is said (NICE NG76, Section Throughout).
Repeat presentations with injuries (NICE NG76, Section Actions when you consider maltreatment).
physicalSigns: Bruises shaped like a hand, ligature, stick, grip or implement; clusters; non-bony sites such as eyes, ears, buttocks (NICE NG76, Section Suspect physical abuse).
Human bite mark unlikely to be from a young child (NICE NG76, Section Suspect physical abuse).
Burns of implement shape, or immersion pattern on buttocks, perineum or lower limbs with sharp borders (NICE NG76, Section Suspect physical abuse).
Injuries on protected areas — back, chest, abdomen, genitals — or ligature marks on neck, wrists or ankles (NICE NG76, Section Suspect physical abuse).
redFlags: Any bruise or petechiae in a non-mobile infant without medical cause (NICE NG76, Section Suspect physical abuse).
Intracranial injury under 3 years with retinal haemorrhage, rib or long-bone fracture, or other inflicted injury (NICE NG76, Section Suspect physical abuse).
Fracture without a suitable explanation, including rib fractures in infants (NICE NG76, Section Suspect physical abuse).
Intra-abdominal or intrathoracic injury without major accidental trauma (NICE NG76, Section Suspect physical abuse).
Carer refusing admission or removing the child against advice.
precipitants: Child not independently mobile (NICE NG76, Section Suspect physical abuse).
Disability — features may overlap with the disability; seek specialist advice (NICE NG76, Section Throughout).
Previous concerns or repeat presentations (NICE NG76, Section Actions when you consider maltreatment).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Suitable, consistent account matching development and mechanism (NICE NG76, Section Unsuitable explanation).
Abnormal clotting; factor VIII deficiency can mimic abusive haemorrhage (ESPR 2025, Section Mimics).

differentials.condition: Metabolic bone disease or osteogenesis imperfecta
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Fractures with rickets, copper deficiency or bone-fragility features (ESPR 2025, Section Mimics).
Young neonate with a delivery explanation (NICE NG76, Section Suspect physical abuse).

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: A serious level of concern (not proof) — refer to the child protection service (NICE NG76, Section Suspect versus consider).
Maltreatment is one possible explanation — look for other features, discuss, gather information and arrange review (NICE NG76, Section Actions when you consider maltreatment).
Implausible, inadequate or inconsistent with the injury, age, development, activities or other accounts, or a cultural explanation (NICE NG76, Section Unsuitable explanation).

clinicalManagement.title: Treat and keep safe
actions: Treat life threats and pain first.
Do not discharge the child to a person or place considered unsafe; admit if needed for safety.

clinicalManagement.title: Take accounts and record
actions: Seek explanations from the carer and the child in an open, non-judgemental way (NICE NG76, Section Throughout).
Record exactly what was seen and heard, from whom and when, and why it concerns you (NICE NG76, Section Throughout).
Judge whether the explanation is suitable (see Diagnostic criteria).

clinicalManagement.title: If you consider maltreatment
actions: Look for other alerting features (NICE NG76, Section Actions when you consider maltreatment).
Discuss with a senior colleague or the hospital child protection lead.
Gather information from other agencies and arrange a review date.

clinicalManagement.title: If you suspect maltreatment — report
actions: Saudi law: any employee who learns of abuse must report it immediately to the employer, and every entity must notify the Ministry or police at once (Executive Regulations, Articles 3.4–3.5).
Report through the hospital child protection team and the Family Protection reporting centre 1919 (24/7) (HRSD Family Protection Department).
Urgent cases go to the police and the Public Prosecution (Executive Regulations, Article 3.6); not reporting carries liability (Article 3.2).

clinicalManagement.title: Image by age
actions: Under 1 year: skeletal survey plus head CT (ESPR 2025, Section Key recommendations).
Follow-up skeletal survey at 11–14 days (ESPR 2025, Section Skeletal survey follow-up).
Siblings and contact children: examine first; under 1 year neuroimaging, 12–24 months skeletal survey (ESPR 2025, Section Contact children).

clinicalManagement.title: Safe disposition
actions: Agree a multiagency safety decision; never discharge only because the carer asks.
The reporter's identity is confidential (Executive Regulations, Article 5).
If a suitable explanation is found, record the actions and outcome (NICE NG76, Section Throughout).

medicationPlan.note: No medicine treats suspected abuse. Treat each injury by its own pathway, with analgesia by age and weight per the hospital paediatric formulary.

learningObjectives: Recognise NICE alerting features of physical abuse.
Know the Saudi legal duty and channels to report.
keyPoints: Bruising in a non-mobile infant is a red flag.
Reporting is a legal duty for every employee in Saudi Arabia.
Skeletal survey is not complete until the 11–14 day follow-up.
pitfalls: Accepting a cultural explanation for harm.
Discharging home while the report is pending.
Forgetting siblings and other children in the home.

patientEducation: Explain to the family, honestly and without blame, that injuries need assessment and that safeguarding referral is a legal duty — unless this would put the child at greater risk.
mdtReferrals: Police and Public Prosecution for urgent cases
dischargeCriteria: Report made and a multiagency safety plan recorded.
Child discharged only to a place agreed as safe.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Follow-up skeletal survey at 11–14 days; child protection team confirms the outcome of the report and arranges paediatric review.
